# meihuizen.ai: We Didn't Start With AI. We Started With a Terminal.
## From an IBM 5110 to enterprise IT
I got my first computer at 12: an IBM 5110, no tutorials, just a terminal and a manual. I taught myself HTML and JavaScript there, building websites for fun. That hobby ran alongside a career in enterprise IT sales, pitching data center, cloud, and SaaS at IBM, SoftLayer, Oracle, and Minitab to buyers who could smell a shallow pitch instantly.
## The pivot to AI-native engineering
Years of pitching taught one habit: understand a product inside out before you present it. Then came the pivot, retraining through Metana's AI Software Engineering program. I now lead meihuizen.ai as an AI-native software engineer, stacking that coding background, sales instinct, and AI training on top of each other. AI isn't a feature here. It's how the work gets built.
## The stack
The stack: TypeScript, Python, React, LLM tooling, agentic workflows, shipped and monitored, not demoed once and forgotten. No computer science degree, and that's fine. Ask about a decision and get a straight answer, including the ones that didn't work first try.
## Small on purpose
I build for quality of life and the freedom to work on my own terms, including as a digital nomad. Small on purpose: close enough to actually understand what you're trying to accomplish, and quick to show up in person when it helps. No far-away delivery team in between.
## No office. On purpose.
There is no office to visit, because there isn't one. The work happens where the work is: at your table, on a call, or in the van, kitted out to build from anywhere with power and a signal.
## "We" means me and my agents
Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Kimi, Mistral, Copilot, BigML, and me. That's the team, and I'd rather say it than let you assume a bench of engineers that doesn't exist.
Every build has two workers on it: someone with a career in enterprise IT behind him, and a model that reads faster than he does and is wrong more confidently. The work is what each one catches the other doing.
Five of them are also the agents I query when I scan someone's website. I know how they read a page because I watch them read mine all day.
## The crew
You don't need thirty employees any more. One person with agents has the reach that used to take a department, and pretending otherwise is just the old org chart with better marketing. So here is the whole roster.
Nico thinks, contemplates, decides, verifies, and signs it
Claude builds, writes, and argues back
ChatGPT second opinion, and register A in a scan
Gemini third read on the same page
Perplexity retrieval, and where a claim came from
Kimi long context, and curiosity
Mistral fifth register, and the European one
Copilot inline completion in the editor
BigML predictive models, and new here
Fritz answers from these pages only, and fetches the leads
Tool names are used to say which tools. No affiliation, partnership or endorsement implied.
## Where the company is
Registered. MB Meihuizen AI, a Lithuanian MB, company code 308157412. The VAT number goes in the footer the day it lands.
This page used to say the opposite. It said registering an empty company to look established is exactly the move I'd flag on a client's site, and that when there was a client there'd be a company. I changed my mind. The old line stays here instead of quietly disappearing, because a page that was never wrong is a page nobody ever edited.
Three things changed it. An MB costs almost nothing to hold open, so the empty-company objection doesn't bite the way it does against a real registration bill. VAT and an entity turned out to be the price of entry to the conversations I want to be in, not the reward for winning them. And Second Audience stopped being an idea. There's a method, there are reports, and there's a page on this site that proves the thing it claims. We're ready to deliver on that promise any day of the week.
Check the company code against the Lithuanian register. Beyond that you have my name, the company address, my email, and public code on GitHub. Verify any of it.
## What I'll tell you about your own site
Second Audience is the scan I run on other people's websites: what an AI agent can actually read, do, and get wrong on your domain. I ran it on this one first. It found things.

pages.title: Agent Fritz: a site agent that only says what your site says | meihuizen.ai
pages.description: An AI agent for your website that answers from your own pages and nothing else, shows its sources, and takes one real action. Try it: it sits in the corner of this page.
pages.text:
# Agent Fritz
The chat in the corner of this page is the product. Ask it anything about meihuizen.ai: it reads the pages it needs, answers from what they say, shows you which ones, and says so when something is not on the site. Named after Nico's dog, who also only brings back what is actually there.
On your website it is the same agent, pointed at your pages, in your languages, with the one action your visitors come for: a quote request, a booking, a lead in your inbox.
Reads before it answersFritz gets an index of the site, not the site. To say anything it has to open the page, and the page it opened is listed under the answer.
Not on the site is an answerAsked for something no page says, it says that, and gives the email address. No estimate, no plausible filler.
One action, after a yesDetails read back, an explicit confirmation, then one email. The server refuses any address the visitor did not type.
## // overview
## Why most website chatbots are a liability
A chatbot that answers from a model's general knowledge fills gaps with something plausible. Under your logo, a plausible wrong price or an invented company detail is your mistake, not the model's. This site keeps a dated correction for exactly that kind of claim on its credentials page: a legal entity stated as fact before it existed.
## Watch it work
Every step streams to the visitor as it happens: which page Fritz is reading, how long it took, and what it read, listed under the answer. The steps are not decoration. They are how a visitor, or you, checks an answer without taking the agent's word for it.
## One action, done properly
Fritz can file a free Second Audience scan request. It asks for a domain and an email address, reads them back, and only sends after the visitor confirms. The check that matters runs on the server, not in the prompt: an address the visitor did not type is refused, so the model cannot invent a lead or “correct” one into someone else's inbox.
## Tested with traps
A fixed set of questions runs against Fritz before a change ships, and the traps are the point: the VAT number that has not been issued yet, the LLC that never existed, the team of engineers that is one person. A wrong answer on any of them means the change does not go out.
## What you get on your site
The same build, pointed at your pages. The knowledge is rebuilt from your content, so editing a page and changing what the agent knows are one change. Your languages, answering in the visitor's. One action wired to your inbox or your system. A test set written for the traps in your business. A spend cap, per-visitor limits, and a switch that turns it off without a deploy. The function runs in Frankfurt and conversations are not logged: the server keeps counts, not content, except the conversation a visitor sends as a request.
## What it costs
Every Fritz is a custom build, so the price follows your content: how many pages, how many languages, which action it takes. Starting from a Second Audience scan, it is priced on the value the scan shows. Without one, tell Nico what your site covers and he will work out a price with you.
## Status
Live on this site in seven languages since September 2026. No client deployment yet: this site is the first, and the one you can test hardest.

pages.title: Off-Grid AI Homestead | meihuizen.ai
pages.description: Off-grid AI farming on two plots 2,256 km apart: Prora on the German Baltic in summer, Castelo Branco in Portugal in winter. Solar Pico node, DWD history.
pages.text:
open the repo
# One Acre, Zero Dependency
Off-grid, AI-driven farming on two plots 2,256 km apart: Prora through summer, Castelo Branco through winter.
A solar-powered field module (Birdbox) collects soil and local weather data. Through the Open-Meteo historical archive API (2006-2026) we bring in twenty years of regional weather history. Eurostat Agriculture Statistics adds regional yield figures, coarse ones though: annual, per hectare and per region, not per bed. The Thun calendar supplies a planting and harvesting calendar based on the position of the moon. This project computes it correctly and tests it, instead of assuming it.
The calculations run in Python. A locally running model (ML/LLM) lays the results side by side and predicts which vegetables and crops give the best yield per planting, when to sow them, and which rotations work best on a small field of 4,000 m².
The aim of this project is to give farmers, hobby growers and families something to hold on to, so they can grow organically at small and large scale, responsibly and successfully, on modern technique and age-old concepts that protect the earth.
status: phase 0. Nothing is built yet. The plan is.
From sensor to scheduler. Storage is the seam.
Two plots, one seasonProra runs through the summer, Castelo Branco through the winter. Between them there is never a month with nothing growing.
Nothing leaves the acreSun to sensor to laptop to schedule. The model runs locally, which is the only way the off-grid claim survives contact with a bill.
The model proposes, Python disposesEvery suggestion passes a deterministic rule set before it becomes a task. What fails the rules is dropped, and the drop is logged.
## // overview
## The question
How much of a small farm's daily decision-making can genuinely off-grid AI handle end to end, from sensor to scheduler?
That is the whole project. Two plots on opposite sides of Europe, worked in alternation, documented publicly through 2026 and 2027. The full write-up, the ADRs and the data sources are in the repo.
## // stack
Pico 2 WMicroPythonPython 3.11SQLiteskyfieldLSTMOllamaBLE / LoRaDWD / IPMAERA5-Land
### AI-Homestead
The repo. Build plan, ADRs, data sources, and the figures on this page.
CODE
### Project overview
Short brief. The two plots, the three commitments, and what each data source can and cannot claim.
PDF
## // where
## Two plots, 2,256 km apart
14.6 degrees of latitude apart. You follow the growing season instead of fighting it.

Latitude54.39 °N
ReferenceDWD Arkona, station 00183, 33 km north

### Castelo Branco winter
WhereCentral Portugal, inland
Latitude39.82 °N
ReferenceIPMA long series, plus ERA5-Land
Winter solstice9.2 h of daylight, sun peaks at 26.7 °
## // commitments
## Three things this project does not compromise on
- 1 · Off-grid means off-grid. No cloud LLM in the daily loop.
- 2 · Every number carries its provenance and its error bars. A €30 sensor claiming ±0.3 pH does not get to report pH to one decimal.
- 3 · The biodynamic calendar is a hypothesis under test, not a scheduling rule.
## // the field node
## A Pico, not a Pi
Prora gets 7.0 hours of daylight at the solstice, sun at 12.2 degrees. That is what the node is sized for.
A duty-cycled Pico runs on roughly sixty times less than an always-on Pi.
Two failure modes kill the node sooner than any sensor: condensation, and charging below zero.
Under 20 metres BLE, above that LoRa. The ingest layer makes that a one-module change.
## // data
## Two plots, two weather services
Prora leans on DWD Arkona, 33 km away, with measured radiation from 1947. Castelo Branco has no equivalent open history and leans on ERA5-Land. That asymmetry is not papered over.
## // the calendar
## The Thun calendar, honestly implemented
Computed from the ephemeris in thirty-minute steps. Sidereal, not tropical.
Tropical signs sit 24 to 25 degrees off the real constellations. Get this wrong and every day type is wrong.
Real IAU boundaries are unequal, so 2027 comes out at 107 root days against 67 flower days.
Ascending and descending is a 27.3-day cycle, entirely separate from waxing and waning at 29.53.
The evidence does not support the trigon effect. The calendar is therefore logged as a covariate and tested, never used as a rule.
## // models
## The LLM proposes, Python disposes
Every number is computed in tested Python. The model selects, prioritises and explains, and returns JSON validated against a schema. What it is aimed at: yield per square metre.
## // roadmap
## Ten phases
September 2026 to October 2027. Every phase has a done-when you can actually check.
MIT for the code. Weather data from DWD (CC BY 4.0), IPMA, and Open-Meteo (CC-BY-4.0). Ephemerides from JPL via skyfield. No copyrighted calendar data is redistributed.

pages.title: Second Audience: AI Agent Website Scan | meihuizen.ai
pages.description: A recurring audit that measures what AI agents like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Perplexity can actually read, do, and get wrong on your website.
pages.text:
# Second Audience
Your website has two kinds of visitor now. One has eyes. The other is agentic AI: it never runs your JavaScript, reads only what your server sends, and then answers questions about you for its visitors, who never open your page. Second Audience measures what that second visitor can actually do.
A service, not a tool. The scan is run by a person and a model working the same case, because the claim being sold is that machines read confidently and get facts wrong, and that is not a claim a machine can certify about itself.
Fetched twiceThe same page with JavaScript and without. What disappears is what a non-rendering crawler never sees.
One fact, four answersA price published once, in a form that invites filling in the rest. Four agents, four numbers, one of them right.
Predictions written firstEighteen written down before an agent was asked anything. Nine of them wrong, and that is in the report.
## // overview
## Seven steps, in this order, and the agents come last
The order is the product. A scan that starts at the agents finds technical imperfections and no money. Every strong finding this year came out of step three: does the same fact appear somewhere else on the domain, worded differently. An FAQ, a stale translation, an orphan page, a press release from four years ago.
## What a finding looks like
A museum's best room costs €299 on weekdays and €325 at the weekend. Its own page says only "from €299". Nine answers from four agents gave €235, €264.50, €277.50, €299 and "between €150 and €350". Not one gave the weekend rate.
A private bank's page title says since 1804. Its own timeline says 1881. The 1804 belongs to the family's textile business, not to the bank. A machine that carries the title away makes the bank seventy-seven years older than it is.
## We publish our own misses
Eighteen predictions written down before a single agent was asked. Nine of them wrong. That is in the report, with the reason. A report that shows only the hits is a sales document and gets read as one.
## A person and a model, working the same case
The machine does the volume: every page fetched twice and compared, every business fact diffed against every other instance of itself on the domain, every cited document opened to see whether its text layer holds what the citation claims. A person makes the three decisions no loop produces: which object carries the revenue, which fact is worth chasing, and whether a citation actually holds. Both are wrong regularly. Each has to answer to the other before anything ships.
## It does not stay fixed
Engines update, pages change, and a claim you have removed keeps being answered for months afterwards. There is a dated measurement of exactly that on this domain. So the work repeats: the same prompts at one week, one month and three months, against the same pages.
## What it costs
The free scan is free. What comes after is priced on the complexity of your site, and every scan report comes with prices for three routes:
- 1 · Do it yourself. Use the implementation report and implement the findings yourself.
- 2 · Full implementation. We handle the complete implementation, including monitoring and the re-scans at one week, one month and three months.
- 3 · Implementation + Agent Fritz. The full implementation, bundled with Agent Fritz on your site, answering visitors from your corrected pages.
With a scan, Fritz is priced on the value the scan shows.
## Status
Seven scans completed. Two of them are now paying clients who arrived as free scans. Reports ship in Dutch and English, with a two-page annex on scope, data, rights and GDPR attached to every one.
## // method
- Dual-render diffing
- robots.txt & UA verification

pages.text:
# Portfolio Website
Not for sale: this is our showcase. What it shows is not the design but the structure: a site built to be read correctly by people and by the AI agents that now answer questions about it.
A terminal, not a templateTraffic lights, a mono path label, a card on a dark ground. The interface states what the site is about before a word is read.
Small behaviours, fenced inThe page is static. A handful of enclosed islands do the interactive work, each one small enough to reason about on its own.
A policy that refuses by defaultOutbound requests are blocked unless the policy names the destination. Security here is a feature of the page, not a header someone remembered.
## // overview
## Not the design. The second audience.
A good designer can make any site look right. That is the half people see. The other half is what an agent reads when someone asks ChatGPT, Gemini or Perplexity about you: which facts are there, how plainly they are stated, whether they can be misread. Most sites only paid for the first half. This one is built for both: facts stated plainly in seven languages, structured data that says the same thing as the page, and a credentials page that replaces the stale claims still in circulation.
## Try it
Ask ChatGPT what meihuizen.ai does and who is behind it. Then ask the same about your own company, and compare. Where the agents get us wrong, we say so: our misses are published on the Second Audience page.
## Want this for your site?
The site is not for sale. The approach is. Tell Nico what your site has to get right, for both audiences, and he will get back to you. Or ask Agent Fritz in the corner; he'll pass it on.
## Terminal-inspired portfolio interface
The site presents professional background, selected work, contact information, and project documentation in a focused terminal-inspired interface. The homepage includes a session-aware type sequence, responsive project cards, and direct navigation to the active work.
## Small JavaScript behaviors with clear boundaries
Vanilla JavaScript powers the typing sequence, form validation, responsive project lightboxes, image cleanup, keyboard dismissal, and body-scroll locking. Shared behavior lives in external same-origin scripts rather than being duplicated across pages.
## Security best practices as a feature
Every page carries a restrictive Content Security Policy as a meta tag, because GitHub Pages sends no custom headers. The only third-party script is Google Analytics. The site avoids unsafe HTML construction, and the contact form validates input, rejects honeypot submissions and sends through a rate-limited serverless function.
## Responsive, accessible presentation
Semantic headings, descriptive image alternatives, keyboard-friendly lightboxes, visible focus states, mobile touch targets, and CSS-centered image crops keep the experience usable across screen sizes.
